query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Under tribological loading in a corrosive environment, high-entropy alloys undergo dynamic amorphization that produces an ultra‐nanocrystalline surface film; this film reduces wear via grain refinement but, due to its high density of reactive grain boundaries, accelerates localized corrosion, thereby governing the coupled tribo‐corrosion response.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, coarse-grained high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with a uniform composition.
generation.intervention: Application of tribological (wear) stress in a corrosive electrolyte to induce dynamic amorphization and near-surface grain refinement.
generation.conditions: Parallel tests: one under tribological loading in an inert environment (to assess wear alone) and one under identical mechanical load in a corrosive medium (e.g., saline solution) to capture the coupled tribo-corrosion response.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer formed by tribo-induced dynamic amorphization.
generation.mechanism: Tribo-induced plastic deformation refines the surface grain structure and creates a protective nano-film that reduces friction and wear. However, the increased density of grain boundaries in the film provides energetically active sites that enhance corrosion in an aggressive medium, leading to a coupled degradation mechanism.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to an inert baseline, samples tested in a corrosive environment will show lower wear rates due to the protective effects of the nano-film, but will exhibit higher corrosion rates because of increased grain boundary activity. The total degradation will reflect a non-additive interaction between these opposing trends.
generation.baseline: The high-entropy alloy under comparable tribological loading in an inert (non-corrosive) environment, where dynamic amorphization still occurs but without the interactive corrosion effects.
generation.boundary: This prediction should hold under moderate tribo-mechanical loads in environments wherein the corrosive species can readily interact with the high-energy boundaries. It may not apply in extreme mechanical conditions that either suppress the formation of the nanocrystalline film or when corrosion is inhibited by environmental constraints.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative balance between the wear-reducing and corrosion-accelerating effects is uncertain due to variations in film thickness, grain boundary reactivity, and the kinetics of corrosion processes.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a set of controlled tests comparing two groups of samples of the same high-entropy alloy. Group A is tested under tribological loading in an inert environment, while Group B is tested under identical mechanical loading in a corrosive (saline) medium. Surface analysis (using TEM or XRD) should be performed pre- and post-test to verify the formation of the ultra-nanocrystalline layer. Measurements should include wear volume, friction coefficient, corrosion current density, and microstructural characterization of the near-surface region.
measurements: Grain size and phase composition (via TEM or XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples under corrosive conditions do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in corrosion rate relative to the inert baseline despite evidence of nanocrystalline film formation, or if the variation in corrosion rate does not correlate with changes in surface grain size, then the hypothesis that dynamic amorphization governs the coupled tribo-corrosion response would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
